title: Nivolumab, ipilimumab, paclitaxel and carboplatin
purpose: This treatment aims to control metastatic squamous non-small-cell lung cancer, help symptoms and extend life. It is usually given without an expectation of cure.

agents.name: Nivolumab
agents.explanation: Nivolumab binds PD-1 on T cells. It prevents signals that can reduce the immune attack on cancer. This can also let immune cells inflame healthy tissues. It is infused every 21 days in this plan.
agents.watch: New breathing, bowel, skin, hormone or other symptoms need prompt advice during or after treatment.

agents.name: Ipilimumab
agents.explanation: Ipilimumab blocks CTLA-4, another control on T-cell activity. It works alongside nivolumab through a different immune checkpoint. It is given every 42 days, so it is absent from each Day 22 visit. Healthy organs can also become inflamed.
agents.watch: Report diarrhoea, tummy pain, rash, severe tiredness, headache or other new symptoms promptly. Keep your immune alert card.
risks: Immune bowel, liver, skin and hormone inflammation

agents.name: Paclitaxel
agents.explanation: Paclitaxel stabilises microtubules, structures cells use during division. It can slow cancer growth but also harm healthy nerves, blood-forming cells and hair follicles. There are two planned doses.
agents.watch: Tell the nurse immediately about infusion symptoms. Report numbness, tingling, fever, painful muscles, mouth sores or diarrhoea.

agents.name: Carboplatin
agents.explanation: Carboplatin forms links in DNA that hinder copying and repair. Healthy tissues can also be harmed. Its dose depends on target exposure (AUC) and measured or estimated kidney function; AUC is not a fixed number of milligrams. There are two planned doses in this regimen.
agents.watch: Report fever, bleeding, nausea, hearing changes or numbness. Tell the nurse immediately about possible allergy during the infusion.

phases.label: Cycle 1: two chemotherapy administrations
phases.detail: One 42-day cycle, chemotherapy Days 1 and 22 only. Cycle 1 lasts 42 days: nivolumab, ipilimumab, paclitaxel and carboplatin on Day 1; nivolumab, paclitaxel and carboplatin on Day 22. These are the only two planned chemotherapy administrations. From Cycle 2, nivolumab is given on Days 1 and 22 and ipilimumab on Day 1.

phases.label: Immune continuation
phases.detail: Until progression, unacceptable toxicity or up to 24 months without progression. Cycle 1 lasts 42 days: nivolumab, ipilimumab, paclitaxel and carboplatin on Day 1; nivolumab, paclitaxel and carboplatin on Day 22. These are the only two planned chemotherapy administrations. From Cycle 2, nivolumab is given on Days 1 and 22 and ipilimumab on Day 1.

timeline.label: Day 1 visit
timeline.text: Includes nivolumab and ipilimumab; chemotherapy in Cycle 1 only

timeline.label: Day 22 visit
timeline.text: Nivolumab; no ipilimumab; final chemotherapy in Cycle 1

timeline.label: Immune symptoms
timeline.text: Any day, including after treatment stops

day_groups.title: Day 1 visit
day_groups.body: Nivolumab and ipilimumab are due. Paclitaxel and carboplatin are also due in Cycle 1 only.
day_groups.action: Report symptoms and confirm the current prescription.

day_groups.title: Between visits
day_groups.body: Follow your prescribed support plan and report new symptoms promptly. Immune effects can occur on any day.
day_groups.action: Keep the oncology contact instructions and immune alert card accessible.

day_groups.title: Day 22 · no ipilimumab
day_groups.body: Nivolumab is due. In Cycle 1 this also includes the second and final chemotherapy administration.
day_groups.action: Confirm active medicines and the right support plan.

day_groups.title: Before the next cycle
day_groups.body: Continue symptom reporting. Later Day 1 visits again include both immune medicines if prescribed.
day_groups.action: Confirm the next appointment and blood tests; do not wait for it if unwell.

support.title: Cycle 1 Days 1 and 22 · chemotherapy-containing visits
support.text: Cycle 1 lasts 42 days: nivolumab, ipilimumab, paclitaxel and carboplatin on Day 1; nivolumab, paclitaxel and carboplatin on Day 22. These are the only two planned chemotherapy administrations. From Cycle 2, nivolumab is given on Days 1 and 22 and ipilimumab on Day 1. Paclitaxel premedication includes corticosteroid and antihistamine treatment, with H2-blocker decisions made by the team. The source allows consultant-directed changes; ask for a written plan for each of the two chemotherapy visits. The team must reconcile paclitaxel allergy-prevention steroids with anti-sickness steroids and the aprepitant interaction into one prescription. Do not add courses or take leftover steroids yourself. Use dedicated carboplatin AUC≥4 NCIS row; no routine olanzapine in that row. Myalgia/arthralgia may need an individual analgesia plan. Both immune medicines can inflame healthy organs during treatment or after it stops. Keep your immune alert card and report new symptoms promptly, including for at least five months after the last dose.

support.title: Cycle 2 onwards · Day 1 nivolumab + ipilimumab
support.text: Both immune medicines can inflame healthy organs during treatment or after it stops. Keep your immune alert card and report new symptoms promptly, including for at least five months after the last dose. Chemotherapy is complete; review and stop induction prophylaxis rather than automatically repeating it.

support.title: Cycle 2 onwards · Day 22 nivolumab alone
support.text: Both immune medicines can inflame healthy organs during treatment or after it stops. Keep your immune alert card and report new symptoms promptly, including for at least five months after the last dose.

questions.a: Cycle 1 lasts 42 days: nivolumab, ipilimumab, paclitaxel and carboplatin on Day 1; nivolumab, paclitaxel and carboplatin on Day 22. These are the only two planned chemotherapy administrations. From Cycle 2, nivolumab is given on Days 1 and 22 and ipilimumab on Day 1.
Continue while appropriate until progression, unacceptable toxicity or up to 24 months without progression. Your team reviews the plan and may delay or stop treatment.

questions.q: What if I miss a support medicine?
questions.a: Ask your oncology team or pharmacist for advice; do not double doses or combine steroid courses yourself.
Your consultant sets the scan plan and reviews symptoms, results and priorities. Side effects do not reliably show cancer response.

questions.q: Can I decide from this guide whether treatment is safe today?
questions.a: No. The team must assess symptoms, blood results, previous reactions and the prescribing protocol.

questions.q: What should I report after treatment stops?
questions.a: Both immune medicines can inflame healthy organs during treatment or after it stops. Keep your immune alert card and report new symptoms promptly, including for at least five months after the last dose.

chapters.title: Why this treatment is offered
chapters.intro: This treatment aims to control metastatic squamous non-small-cell lung cancer, help symptoms and extend life. It is usually given without an expectation of cure.

items.title: What does the diagnosis mean?
items.text: Squamous NSCLC is a lung-cancer histology. Metastatic means it has spread; the team confirms EGFR/ALK results and first-line suitability.

items.title: What are the alternatives?
items.text: Ask about other systemic options, trials and symptom-focused care in the context of your cancer, health and priorities.

chapters.title: Before the first visit
chapters.intro: Paclitaxel premedication includes corticosteroid and antihistamine treatment, with H2-blocker decisions made by the team. The source allows consultant-directed changes; ask for a written plan for each of the two chemotherapy visits.

items.title: Your usual health
items.text: Describe usual bowel movements, breathing, energy and skin; report autoimmune illness, infection, nerve symptoms and every medicine or supplement.

items.title: Practical preparation
items.text: Arrange blood tests, transport and support at home. Keep treatment names, urgent contacts and your immune alert card available.

chapters.title: Alternating treatment visits
chapters.intro: Cycle 1 lasts 42 days: nivolumab, ipilimumab, paclitaxel and carboplatin on Day 1; nivolumab, paclitaxel and carboplatin on Day 22. These are the only two planned chemotherapy administrations. From Cycle 2, nivolumab is given on Days 1 and 22 and ipilimumab on Day 1.

items.title: Duration
items.text: Continue while appropriate until progression, unacceptable toxicity or up to 24 months without progression. Your team reviews the plan and may delay or stop treatment.

items.title: Time in the unit
items.text: Nivolumab over 30 minutes, then ipilimumab over 30 minutes on Day 1 only. Paclitaxel over three hours, then carboplatin over 30 minutes on both Cycle 1 treatment days. Ipilimumab vital signs are checked every 30 minutes during infusion and for an hour afterwards. Blood tests, preparation and observation add to time in the unit.

chapters.title: Checks before and during treatment
chapters.intro: Blood count, kidney and liver tests before each treatment; glucose and thyroid tests before each 42-day cycle. Cortisol and neuropathy checks when indicated.

items.title: Before starting
items.text: Baseline FBC, renal/liver profile, glucose and TFTs; hepatitis B surface antigen and hepatitis C RNA. GFR for carboplatin; audiology/CrCl and neuropathy assessment when indicated.

items.title: New symptoms
items.text: Extra tests may be needed between visits. Routine blood results alone cannot exclude every immune effect.

items.title: Response
items.text: Scans follow the consultant plan; discuss benefit, uncertainty and what would lead to changing treatment.

chapters.title: Treatment effects
chapters.intro: Both immune medicines can inflame healthy organs during treatment or after it stops. Keep your immune alert card and report new symptoms promptly, including for at least five months after the last dose.

items.title: Bowel, lungs and skin
items.text: New diarrhoea, tummy pain, blood/mucus in stool, cough, breathlessness, blistering or peeling skin need prompt assessment.

items.title: Hormones, heart, muscles and nerves
items.text: Unusual weakness, headache, dizziness, marked thirst, frequent urination, chest pain, palpitations, drooping eyelids or difficulty swallowing/breathing need urgent advice. Several organs can be inflamed together.

items.title: Chemotherapy effects
items.text: Paclitaxel/carboplatin can cause low blood counts, infection, hair loss, neuropathy, muscle pain, nausea and infusion reactions. Report symptoms before another dose.

chapters.title: Support medicines and self-care
chapters.intro: The team must reconcile paclitaxel allergy-prevention steroids with anti-sickness steroids and the aprepitant interaction into one prescription. Do not add courses or take leftover steroids yourself.

items.title: Your plan
items.text: Paclitaxel premedication includes corticosteroid and antihistamine treatment, with H2-blocker decisions made by the team. The source allows consultant-directed changes; ask for a written plan for each of the two chemotherapy visits.

items.title: When unwell
items.text: Follow your oncology emergency instructions for fever, shivering or sudden illness even with a normal temperature. Severe breathing difficulty, chest pain, collapse or confusion needs emergency care.

chapters.title: After treatment and daily life
chapters.intro: Both immune medicines can inflame healthy organs during treatment or after it stops. Keep your immune alert card and report new symptoms promptly, including for at least five months after the last dose.

items.title: Reproductive advice
items.text: Discuss pregnancy, breastfeeding, fertility and contraception before treatment. Effective contraception is needed for at least five months after the last nivolumab dose; ask about your individual plan.

items.title: Living with treatment
items.text: Ask for help with fatigue, appetite, pain, breathlessness, work and emotional concerns. Follow-up continues for unresolved effects and any long-term hormone replacement.

evidence.title: Why this treatment is offered
evidence.intro: The combined strategy improved survival compared with chemotherapy in the trial population, with some durable responses. Benefits and harms vary between people.
evidence.interpretation: Trial results compare groups and cannot predict your personal benefit. Discuss how the study population relates to your cancer and health.
evidence.population: 719 previously untreated adults with stage IV/recurrent NSCLC without sensitising EGFR/ALK alterations; mixed squamous and non-squamous histologies.
evidence.limitations: No personal survival estimate or cross-trial ranking.

anatomy: Unusual weakness, headache, dizziness, thirst or passing much more urine.
New cough or breathlessness needs prompt assessment; infection or cancer can cause similar symptoms.
Chest pain, racing heartbeat, fainting or new muscle weakness needs urgent assessment.
Yellow eyes/skin, dark urine or abnormal tests can signal inflammation.
Kidney tests matter; report less urine, swelling or difficulty drinking.
Report new diarrhoea, pain, blood/mucus or mouth ulcers; do not assume ordinary chemotherapy upset.
Report spreading rash, blistering, numbness, weakness or difficulty swallowing.
Fever, shivers, sudden illness or unusual bleeding need immediate oncology advice.
